hero.headline: Advocate says warnings preceded St. Lucie County’s historic flooding
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County resident and water-policy advocate Nyla Pipes said warnings about flooding risks had been raised weeks before the county’s historic early-November flooding, with o
hero.body:
St. Lucie County resident and water-policy advocate Nyla Pipes said warnings about flooding risks had been raised weeks before the county’s historic early-November flooding, with other concerns stretching back years. Speaking at a South Florida Water Management District board meeting after the flooding, Pipes challenged the idea that the danger had arrived without warning.

 The flooding damaged hundreds of homes after more than three days of rain dropped over a foot of water on parts of the county, with some locations recording as much as 17 inches. More heavy rain this week has renewed concerns about the drainage system’s capacity. Schools were closed Wednesday.

 Responsibility for drainage is divided among the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the water management district, the county, cities, local water-control districts and homeowners’ associations. Which agency handles a problem depends on the canal or drainage system involved. Water typically travels through ditches and canals toward the St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon before reaching the ocean.

 During the flooding, unusually high tides restricted that flow. County Commissioner Cathy Townsend said residents called as water rose, asking what officials were doing. She said she could tell them only that floodgates were open and water was moving, despite the worsening conditions.

 At the district meeting, board member Thomas Hurley described the flooding as a warning that infrastructure maintenance is becoming more important as water levels rise. Fellow board member Jay Steinle said shortcomings in forecasting equipment had left the district without enough advance notice to lower canal levels and prepare. Pipes, however, said concerns had already been raised.

 Townsend has called for better maintenance of county canals and ditches and criticized the district’s timing in opening a canal. She said she later learned that an environmental concern had caused the delay. Townsend also acknowledged that earlier openings might not have prevented flooding, given the amount of water the system faced.

 The damage revealed weaknesses in newer planned developments, including Tradition. In its Vitalia neighborhood, floodwater submerged streets, stranded vehicles and left some residents without electricity for days. Tradition was built using the existing canal network, and developers were not required to construct a new canal, a possible factor in the community’s drainage problems.

 The flooding also created financial concerns for homeowners. Many affected properties were outside areas FEMA designates as having a high flood risk, where flood insurance is generally required for federally backed mortgages. Some owners outside those zones may not have carried flood coverage to help pay for repairs.

cards.headline: Volunteers remove flood-damaged drywall from Jensen Beach's Skyline Drive homes
cards.teaser: Volunteers removed flood-damaged drywall Thursday from homes in Jensen Beach's Skyline Drive neighborhood, with demolition and cleanup targeted for completion Saturday. Project LIF
cards.body:
Volunteers removed flood-damaged drywall Thursday from homes in Jensen Beach's Skyline Drive neighborhood, with demolition and cleanup targeted for completion Saturday. Project LIFT and community partners arrived Thursday morning, two weeks after flooding damaged homes in the neighborhood. Some families are staying with friends or in hotels as Thanksgiving approaches, said Stephen Leighton, the volunteer coordinator with 25 United Disaster Relief.

 Leighton said 17 homes in the community sustained water damage. County inspectors are helping homeowners understand the repairs and permits they need. Volunteers working with 25 United carried damaged drywall out of homes and into dumpsters, which are quickly filling as cleanup continues. “So, Project LIFT, working with 25 United, came in, took all the drywall off the walls, took it outside to the dumpster,” Leighton said. Waterlines remained visible on the exposed studs.

 Susan Destafney's home is completely gutted, and water damage has left her unable to live there. “We have a long way to go until we rebuild, you know. We’ve demoed, and we’ve got a long future ahead of us, and I know that God will be there for us and everything is going to be good,” Destafney said. Mark Burner, who has lived in the neighborhood for 40 years, expressed gratitude for the volunteers helping residents recover.

 Bob Zaccheo, CEO of Project LIFT, emphasized the rebuilding work beyond demolition. “To see these houses getting repaired and torn apart, torn down, is one thing, but built back is a whole other,” Zaccheo said. Leighton said the efforts are being coordinated with state and federal representatives, with the goal of finishing demolition and cleanup by Saturday.

cards.headline: Woods scores twice in Vero Beach's playoff win over Fort Pierce Central
cards.teaser: Vero Beach High School junior Latravious Woods totaled more than 100 yards and scored two touchdowns in last week's playoff victory over Fort Pierce Central, helping the Fighting I
cards.body:
Vero Beach High School junior Latravious Woods totaled more than 100 yards and scored two touchdowns in last week's playoff victory over Fort Pierce Central, helping the Fighting Indians continue their push for a state title. The wide receiver has played in the postseason in each of his three high school seasons and was part of Vero Beach's run to the state championship game in 2025. Now, he hopes to help the team return to that stage and win the title, while concentrating on the next game rather than looking too far ahead.

 Woods grew up watching the Fighting Indians from the stands before joining the team as a freshman. Since then, he has developed into a player his coaches and teammates rely on, with responsibilities that extend beyond catching passes. Vero Beach head coach Lenny Jankowski said Woods gives the team options in how it uses him.

 "He's a guy that you hope to get the ball in his hands, however it needs to happen," Jankowski said. "And he's got some position versatility." His production against Fort Pierce Central added another strong performance to his role in the offense during Vero Beach's playoff pursuit.

 Woods also takes responsibility for helping teammates understand the program's expectations and keeping their spirits up. "I know a lot about the program and how things and how coaches want things done," Woods said. "I just make sure everybody's just up-notch and like we all on the same level.

 Nobody heads down." That approach carries into his effort on plays designed for someone else. "Even though I don't have the ball in my hands, I just got to go 100% every play because, you know, if I was to have the ball in my hand, I would want somebody to go 100% for me," he said.

 For Woods, giving that effort is a way to support the people around him, not just improve his own numbers. "So I'm going to give 100% for my teammates and my coaches because I want the same when I have the ball," he said. After experiencing a state championship appearance, Woods wants to finish the next trip with a title for the team he once watched as a child.

 "Being back there this year and just finishing it all the way this time, it would feel so great," Woods said. "And I know the whole Vero community would love it."

cards.headline: Hobe Sound singer joins Matthew Morrison for surprise duet at Maltz Jupiter Theatre
cards.teaser: Emily Rynasko learned that morning she would sing with the Broadway and "Glee" star that night after an FAA ground stop disrupted his ensemble's travel.
cards.body:
Hobe Sound singer Emily Rynasko joined Broadway and "Glee" star Matthew Morrison for a surprise duet at the Maltz Jupiter Theatre after an FAA ground stop kept much of his ensemble from reaching the venue. Rynasko, who began training at the theater as a child, learned about the performance that morning.

 Morrison sent Rynasko a text asking her to sing with him onstage. She had watched "Glee" when she was younger, including Morrison's portrayal of William Schuester. "I found out about 9:30 in the morning, and the show was at 7:30 that night," Rynasko said.

 Rynasko grew up in Hobe Sound and credited her musical training with helping her prepare for the same-day performance. "Learning sight-reading music and just using my ear. It's being a trained musician that's part of your job," Rynasko said. She described the Maltz Jupiter Theatre as her home and the people there as family, crediting them with helping shape the woman she has become.

 Onstage, Rynasko sang "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" alongside Morrison and approached the duet as she would another professional performance. "I was a lot calmer than I thought I would be because I treated it like any other show that I had done," Rynasko said. She also spoke about honoring the teachers, community, friends and family who have been part of her journey. "That's what brings me joy and carries me through."

 Rynasko grew up in Hobe Sound and credited her musical training with helping her prepare for the same-day performance. "Learning sight-reading music and just using my ear. It's being a trained musician that's part of your job," Rynasko said. She described the Maltz Jupiter Theatre as her home and the people there as family, crediting them with helping shape the woman she has become.

 Onstage, Rynasko sang "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" alongside Morrison and approached the duet as she would another professional performance. "I was a lot calmer than I thought I would be because I treated it like any other show that I had done," Rynasko said. She also spoke about honoring the teachers, community, friends and family who have been part of her journey. "That's what brings me joy and carries me through."

hero.headline: Advocate says warnings preceded St. Lucie County’s historic flooding
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County resident and water-policy advocate Nyla Pipes said warnings about flooding risks had been raised weeks before the county’s historic early-November flooding, with o
hero.body:
St. Lucie County resident and water-policy advocate Nyla Pipes said warnings about flooding risks had been raised weeks before the county’s historic early-November flooding, with other concerns stretching back years. Speaking at a South Florida Water Management District board meeting after the flooding, Pipes challenged the idea that the danger had arrived without warning.

 The flooding damaged hundreds of homes after more than three days of rain dropped over a foot of water on parts of the county, with some locations recording as much as 17 inches. More heavy rain this week has renewed concerns about the drainage system’s capacity. Schools were closed Wednesday.

 Responsibility for drainage is divided among the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the water management district, the county, cities, local water-control districts and homeowners’ associations. Which agency handles a problem depends on the canal or drainage system involved. Water typically travels through ditches and canals toward the St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon before reaching the ocean.

 During the flooding, unusually high tides restricted that flow. County Commissioner Cathy Townsend said residents called as water rose, asking what officials were doing. She said she could tell them only that floodgates were open and water was moving, despite the worsening conditions.

 At the district meeting, board member Thomas Hurley described the flooding as a warning that infrastructure maintenance is becoming more important as water levels rise. Fellow board member Jay Steinle said shortcomings in forecasting equipment had left the district without enough advance notice to lower canal levels and prepare. Pipes, however, said concerns had already been raised.

 Townsend has called for better maintenance of county canals and ditches and criticized the district’s timing in opening a canal. She said she later learned that an environmental concern had caused the delay. Townsend also acknowledged that earlier openings might not have prevented flooding, given the amount of water the system faced.

 The damage revealed weaknesses in newer planned developments, including Tradition. In its Vitalia neighborhood, floodwater submerged streets, stranded vehicles and left some residents without electricity for days. Tradition was built using the existing canal network, and developers were not required to construct a new canal, a possible factor in the community’s drainage problems.

 The flooding also created financial concerns for homeowners. Many affected properties were outside areas FEMA designates as having a high flood risk, where flood insurance is generally required for federally backed mortgages. Some owners outside those zones may not have carried flood coverage to help pay for repairs.
